concepts.def: Departs with bonding e- pair; e.g. Br-.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Nucleophile attacks C from opposite side to leaving group. Transition state has partial bonds to both.

Rate = k[R-X][Nu-]. Inversion of configuration (Walden inversion). Best with 1° R-X due to low steric hindrance.

Step 1 (slow): R-X -> R+ + X-. Step 2 (fast): R+ + Nu- -> R-Nu.

Rate = k[R-X] only. Tertiary R-X favoured (stable carbocation). Racemic mixture from planar cation.

Tertiary, polar protic solvent, weak Nu -> SN1. Primary, polar aprotic, strong Nu -> SN2.

Secondary is in-between. Bulky Nu favours SN1 (or E1); strong Nu/base + heat favours elimination.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary halogenoalkanes typically react via SN1 rather than SN2?
options: The order of reaction is always equal to the number of reactants in the equation.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
The tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect), making the SN1 pathway favourable.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN1 because they are more reactive in every way.

mcqs.q: What does a curly arrow in an organic mechanism represent?
options: A curly arrow shows the direction in which heat is flowing in the reaction.
The movement of a pair of electrons from where they are to where they end up.
A curly arrow shows the movement of an atom from one position to another.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.

mcqs.q: Can you determine the order of a reaction with respect to a reactant from the balanced equation?
options: A curly arrow shows the direction in which heat is flowing in the reaction.
No — orders must be determined experimentally; they often differ from the stoichiometric coefficients.
The order of reaction is always equal to the number of reactants in the equation.
The order of reaction with respect to each reactant equals its coefficient in the balanced equation.
